source.title: Half a dozen famous unsolved problems in mathematics with a dozen suggestions on how to try to solve them

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many twin-prime pairs, meaning infinitely many prime numbers p such that p+2 is also prime? In the formulation emphasized in this paper, if {p_n} denotes the sequence of primes that belong to twin-prime pairs, can one prove that the canonical product over those primes has order exactly 1, equivalently by showing that the order of the product over n of (1 - z/p_n) is at least 1 or cannot be less than 1?

evidence.quote: However, no one knows, whether the number of Twin Primes ... is finite or infinite.
The Twin Prime Conjecture, TPC, states that the number of Twin Primes is infinite.
My first suggestion is, of course, to try to show Order of Q (1 − z/pn) ≥ 1 or that the Order of Q (1 − z/pn) cannot be less than 1.

accepted.question_text: Can one prove the Twin Prime Conjecture by choosing an appropriate entire function F(z) so that multiplying F(z) by the canonical product over twin-prime factors, specifically the product over n of (1 - z/p_n)e^{z/p_n}, forces the product over n of (1 - z/p_n) to have order exactly 1? The paper notes that the natural candidate e^{-Bz}, where B is Brun's constant, does not immediately work because one would need a theorem covering products of entire functions of the same order and the same type.

evidence.quote: Using Brun’s result, I have shown [10] that TPC equivalent to: Order Q of (1 − z/pn) = 1.
Now my second suggestion revolves about trying to multiply Q (1− z/pn)e^{z/pn} by the appropriate entire function to show that Order of Q (1 − z/pn) = 1.

accepted.question_text: Does every even integer greater than or equal to 4 equal the sum of two prime numbers? The paper presents this as Euler's restatement of Goldbach's conjecture and highlights the stronger research objective of turning Chen's theorem, which only gives a prime plus a product of at most two primes for sufficiently large even integers, into a proof that every sufficiently large even integer is actually a sum of two primes.

evidence.quote: Euler restated the conjecture as: Every EVEN number ≥ 4 is the sum of two primes.
one suggestion is to strengthen Chen’s theorem to show that every large EVEN integer is the sum of two primes.

accepted.question_text: Can one explicitly determine a threshold integer n0 greater than 4×10^18 such that every even integer n > n0 is a sum of two primes, and then verify by computation that every remaining even integer m with 4×10^18 < m ≤ n0 is also a sum of two primes? This is posed in the paper as a concrete route to resolving the even Goldbach conjecture by combining a theoretical bound with exhaustive computation.

evidence.quote: Oliveira e Silva, Herzog, and Pardi [27] who have verified using computers that every even integer up to (4)10^18 is the sum of two primes

another suggestion is to explicitly find a positive integer n0 such that every EVEN number n > n0 is the sum of two primes (presumably n0 > (4)10^18) and then check that the desired result holds for all even numbers m with (4)10^18 < m ≤ n0 using a (super)computer or many (super)computers working in parallel.

accepted.question_text: Do all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have real part 1/2? Equivalently, if ξ(z)=1/2·z(z−1)π^{-z/2}Γ(z/2)ζ(z) is the completed zeta function, are all zeros of ξ(z) located on the critical line Re(z)=1/2?

evidence.quote: In the same paper Riemann conjectured that ALL non-trivial zeros of his zeta function have real part equal to 1/2. This has been known as the Riemann Hypothesis.
The Riemann Hypothesis using the completed zeta function. ALL zeros of ξ(z) are on the critical line Re(z) = 1/2.

accepted.question_text: Can the Riemann Hypothesis be proved by constructing a globally meaningful proxy for Euler's product formula that remains usable inside the critical strip, where the ordinary Euler product does not converge in the naive way? The paper quotes this as a suggested necessary ingredient for progress on the hypothesis.

evidence.quote: A technique that allows the Euler product in the critical strip seems unavoidable. For example, a proxy for the Euler product that has a global meaning.

accepted.question_text: Can one determine an exact closed-form value for ζ(3), and more broadly for ζ(n) at odd integers n ≥ 3? The paper stresses that no exact value of the zeta function at any odd integer at least 3 is known, then focuses on the specific problem of identifying the exact value of the convergent series sum over n of 1/n^3.

evidence.quote: No exact value of the zeta function at any odd integer ≥ 3 is known
Here we specialize by considering the zeta function at 3. Thus the exact value that Σ∞ n=1 1/n^3 converges to is one of the most notorious problems that did not even yield to Euler.

accepted.question_text: Can one obtain the exact value of ζ(3) either by finding an integer relation among the constants in the author's representation using the LLL algorithm and then proving that relation rigorously, or by exploiting the series identity ζ(3)=4(-1+ln 4)−Σ_{n≥1} 1/(n^3(4n^2−1)) to derive a closed-form evaluation? These are presented in the paper as two explicit routes to solving the ζ(3) problem.

evidence.quote: One suggestion is to use the LLL algorithm in the Computer Algebra System Maple to find an integer relation which is then proved mathematically.
Consequently, ζ(3) = 4(−1 + ln 4) − Σ∞ 1 1/(n^3(4n^2 − 1)). So another suggestion pops up and that is to use the latter series, as a means, to find the exact value of ζ(3).

accepted.question_text: If a, b, and c are positive integers and x, y, and z are integers greater than 2 satisfying a^x + b^y = c^z, must a, b, and c have a common prime factor? Equivalently, when x, y, z > 2 and a, b, c are pairwise coprime positive integers, is the equation a^x + b^y = c^z impossible?

evidence.quote: states that the only solutions to the equation a^x + b^y = c^z, when a, b and c are positive integers, and x, y and z are positive integers greater than two, are those in which a, b and c have a common prime factor.
Suppose x, y and z are positive integers greater than two. Then the equation a^x + b^y = c^z, has no solution when a, b and c are positive integers that are coprime.

accepted.question_text: Can each of the listed RSA challenge numbers—specifically RSA-896, RSA-1024, RSA-1536, and RSA-2048—be factored into its two prime factors? The paper presents these factorizations as open computational number-theory challenges and suggests imitating the methods previously used to factor RSA-129 and RSA-768.

evidence.quote: Factoring, however, is not always easy and below are some challenge numbers with prizes for finding their TWO prime factors:

One suggestion is to imitate what was done in [23] when, in 1994, RSA-129 ... was factored ... or [21] when, on December 12, 2009, RSA-768 ... was factored into the product of two 116-digit prime numbers:

trace.notes: Mapped the PDF as a six-problem survey with main problem regions in sections 2 through 7: twin primes, Goldbach, Riemann Hypothesis, zeta values at odd arguments, Beal conjecture, and RSA challenge numbers.
Extracted the explicit Twin Prime Conjecture statement and the first entire-function suggestion from page 3.
Expanded the second twin-prime suggestion into a standalone question by inlining the product representation and the issue about same-order same-type entire-function products.
Captured the binary Goldbach conjecture and the explicit suggestion to strengthen Chen's theorem.
Rewrote the computational Goldbach route as a self-contained threshold-and-verification problem.
Captured both the classical and ξ-function formulations of the Riemann Hypothesis.
Converted Ricardo Marco's recommendation into a direct research question about a critical-strip Euler-product proxy.
Captured the explicit unsolved-status statement for odd zeta values and the paper's focus on ζ(3).
Merged the two explicit ζ(3) suggestions into one canonical self-contained question because both target the same exact-value problem.
Captured the Beal conjecture and its contrapositive restatement as the same underlying open problem.
Captured the RSA challenge-number factoring tasks as explicit open computational problems listed in section 7.
All accepted questions were checked for self-containedness, evidence coverage, and no-new-facts compliance; no unresolved references remained after rewriting.
